t: 2170. Minimum Operations to Make the Array Alternating
o: Alternating means even-indexed entries all share one value and odd-indexed entries share another, with the two values different. Even and odd positions are independent, so on each side change everything except the most frequent value. The only interaction: if both sides pick the same value, one side must fall back to its second-most-frequent value (or 0 changes on that side if it has a single distinct value). Answer = n minus the best kept count. Example 2: evens [1,2,2] keep 2 (twice), odds [2,2] keep 2, conflict resolved by keeping 1 on the even side -> 5 - 3 = 2.
k: Even and odd halves can be optimized independently except for a value collision.
Track the top two frequencies per side; on collision the answer is n - max(top_even + second_odd, second_even + top_odd).

a.i: Count frequencies on each half, extract the two largest counts, and combine according to whether the leaders collide.
s: Counter the even-indexed and odd-indexed subsequences.
Get (top, second) counts for each side.
If tops differ, answer n - top_e - top_o; otherwise n - max(top_e + second_o, second_e + top_o), treating missing seconds as 0.
a.t: O(n) — one counting pass per half plus linear top-two extraction

a.i: Same idea, but sort each half's frequency list descending and read off the top two explicitly — easier to reason about and debug.
s: Counter each half and sort its frequency values descending.
Pad with 0 so index 1 always exists.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting the frequency lists dominates

w: Edge cases: a half with a single distinct value has second = 0 (then that side must change everything if the leaders collide); arrays of length 1 need 0 operations. Pitfall: forgetting the collision case entirely — [1,2,2,2,2] is the classic trap. Follow-up: alternating over period 3 (three independent residue classes, pairwise-distinct constraint handled greedily).
